These thinkers separated Aristotle’s logic from its substantive meaning—from its relation to knowledge—and reduced it to one aspect alone: pure form.
The great social philosopher Ibn Khaldūn clearly recognized this kind of “change” in Aristotle’s logic, as he called it.

After reviewing the contents of Aristotle’s eight logical works, discussing their translation “within the Islamic community,” and describing how Muslim philosophers circulated them through commentaries and summaries, Ibn Khaldūn wrote:
“…Then the later scholars came and changed the terminology of logic.”
He then identified the exact point where this change had taken place:

“…They discussed the syllogism only in terms of its general ability to produce conclusions, without regard to its subject matter. They removed the study of the syllogism according to its material content—that is, the five books on Demonstration, Dialectic, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Sophistics. Some of them may touch on a little of this, but only briefly. They neglected these works almost as though they did not exist, even though they are the most important and essential part of the discipline.”
Whatever position this group of traditionalists took toward Aristotle’s logic, they still used it, even in their attacks on philosophy and philosophers.
They used mainly its purely formal side.
Al-Ghazālī himself is the clearest example.

Despite his famous hostility toward philosophy and philosophers and his historical campaign against them, he not only wrote several works devoted specifically to formal logic. He also placed a purely logical introduction at the beginning of his al-Mustaṣfā.
There, in very firm language, he states that anyone who does not understand the logical questions covered in that introduction cannot be trusted in his knowledge.

Before al-Ghazālī, Imam al-Ḥaramayn, one of the leading early Ashʿarites (d. 478 AH), had already used Aristotelian logic in his discussions of the principles of Islamic law, despite disagreeing with parts of that logic.
Among later thinkers of this traditionalist current were Najm al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 606 AH/early thirteenth century) and Afḍal al-Dīn al-Khūnajī (d. 646 AH/mid-thirteenth century).
Both gave considerable attention to logic in their writings, but in the way Ibn Khaldūn described above.
The Andalusian thinker Ibn Ḥazm (d. 456 AH/c. 1064) took a similar position toward Aristotle’s logic.

Although his Ẓāhirī school made him a strict traditionalist, he defended logic and wrote the well-known work Approximation to the Limits of Logic and an Introduction to It through Everyday Examples and Juristic Expressions.
His book was, in practice, an answer to the hostility shown toward logic by the jurists and later theologians of his time.
C — Theoretical Differences Between Two Kinds of Logic
Alongside these two positions, there were also specific theoretical differences between Aristotle’s logic and the logic used by some schools of jurisprudence, kalām, and mystical philosophy.
These differences were another form of the adaptation that Aristotle’s logic—and ancient logic more generally—underwent through cultural interaction within the historical conditions of the period.
On this question, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, for example, rejects the idea that a definition must be made up of a genus and a differentia.
This goes against Aristotle’s understanding of definition.
An Aristotelian definition is made up of genus and differentia because its purpose is to answer the question “What is it?”—that is, to explain “the essence of the thing and its true nature.”
Al-Rāzī’s position comes from his complete denial that universals exist outside the mind.
Most Ashʿarite theologians took the same position.
For them, universals were nothing more than “conventional names.”
ʿUthmān Amīn argues that they derived this view from Stoicism.
Can we see a connection here between this position and the nominalism known in medieval Europe?

One reason for thinking so is that thinkers who agreed with al-Rāzī in rejecting Aristotle’s theory of definition also argued that a definition does no more than explain the meaning of a name. It does not reveal the essence of the thing being defined, as it does in Aristotelian logic.

“…The most rigorous theoretical thinkers know that the purpose of a definition is to distinguish the thing defined from other things, just as a name does. Its purpose is not to form a conception of the thing or reveal its true nature. Only the followers of Greek logic, the followers of Aristotle, make that claim…”
We find another position on definition in the philosophy of the Illuminationist mystic al-Suhrawardī, known as “the slain young man.”
He too opposed Aristotle’s theory of definition, but for a different reason.

In al-Suhrawardī’s view, an Aristotelian definition is not a productive tool for gaining knowledge, because the property used to distinguish the thing being defined does not actually reveal its true nature.
Using the Aristotelian method, we might define it as an animal—the genus—that neighs—the distinguishing property.
But while we already understand what an animal is, “neighing” is still not understood if it exists only in the very thing we are trying to define: the horse.
For someone who has never seen a horse, saying that a horse is “an animal that neighs” therefore tells them very little.
Al-Suhrawardī concludes that a proper definition must list all the essential characteristics which, taken together, belong only to the thing being defined.
The Arab-Islamic philosophers, by contrast—especially the most famous among them, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd—accepted Aristotle’s theory of definition.
The main reason was that they accepted the existence of universals.
They believed that universals explain the true nature and essence of things. For them, universals were therefore not merely conventional names.
Ibn Sīnā, for example, bases his treatment of the five universals—genus, species, differentia, property, and general accident—on the fact that they answer the question “What is it?”
In other words, they belong directly to the definition of a thing’s true nature and essence.
“Every universal predicate said of what falls under it in answer to the question ‘What is it?’…”
And on the meaning of definition itself, he writes:

“A definition is a statement that indicates the essence of a thing. There is no doubt that it must contain all the elements that constitute that essence, and so it must necessarily be made up of its genus and differentia…”
But Ibn Sīnā did not limit definition to this Aristotelian form.
He also described three other kinds: definition by indication, definition by wording, and definition through a necessary or accompanying property—the last of which is known as rasm.
This kind of definition is based on “necessary attributes that constitute the thing’s existence, even if they do not constitute its essence or concept.”
Unlike the Aristotelian definition, this last kind relies on induction.
This was Ibn Sīnā’s addition to Aristotle’s theory.
Second — The question of the excluded middle:
Aristotelian logical demonstration rests on two basic principles.
The first is the principle that two contradictory propositions cannot both be true.
The second is the principle that two contradictory propositions cannot both be false. This is also known as the law of the excluded middle.
Arab logicians did not disagree with the first principle.
But some did reject the second.
One example was Abū Sulaymān al-Sijistānī the Logician (d. 380 AH/990 CE), the teacher of Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī.

While trying to prove the existence of God, al-Sijistānī argued that the only possible path was to deny an attribute of God and also deny the absence of that attribute; to deny a limit and also deny the absence of a limit.
He realized that this would provoke the objection that he was combining contradictions.
His answer was that two propositions count as contradictory only when one is affirmative and the other negative.
That condition, he said, did not apply here, because both propositions were negative.
There is therefore no contradiction, he argued, between saying “not described” and “not not-described.”
The contradiction would be between “described” and “not described.”
We have not combined two contradictions by saying that God is living and not living. We have instead rejected both sides and said: neither described nor not-described.
Al-Sijistānī therefore defended himself against the charge of accepting two contradictions at once.
But he openly accepted the possibility of rejecting both sides of a contradiction, and he saw nothing problematic in doing so.
He therefore directly rejected the principle that both contradictory alternatives cannot be excluded—the principle of the excluded middle.
In Aristotle’s logic, causality is one of the basic principles underlying demonstrative reasoning.
The relationship between cause and effect in the existence of things, events, and people is treated as necessary and self-evident to reason.
The validity of logical demonstrations depends on this necessary and rational connection.
On this question, the Ashʿarites and some Muʿtazilite theologians rejected the law of causality at its foundation.
Their position differed from that of the best-known Arab philosophers, who relied on causality in their studies of both logic and philosophy.

“Whoever denies causes denies reason itself. The discipline of logic assumes that causes and effects exist, and that complete knowledge of effects is possible only through knowledge of their causes. To deny these things is to destroy knowledge and abolish it.”
The disagreement here was not merely theoretical.
At its core, it was ideological.

To deny the law of causality is, as Ibn Rushd said, one form of denying reason. It also means denying reason’s role in the development of science. And denying the development of science ultimately means denying the development of society.

The Ashʿarites generally believed that accepting causality as a rational and logical law would threaten their belief that God continually creates human actions, natural events, and natural things anew at every moment.
In their view, these actions and events can be divided into separate parts with no necessary causal connection between them.
God creates each part separately and independently.
They explained that what appears to us to be a logical sequence between these separate events is not really a logical sequence at all.
It is not a causal connection.
It is a “chance” phenomenon—a kind of coincidence.
To soften this idea of coincidence, the Ashʿarites developed their well-known theory of habit.
They used it to explain why things and events appear to be causally connected.
Take the connection between touching fire and being burned.
The Ashʿarites argued that this connection is only apparent, not real.
We think it is causal because we have repeatedly seen the two events occur together. Habit then leads us to judge that fire is the cause of burning.
The theory of habit was not only a defense of the idea of continuous renewed creation. It was also a defense of divine miracles.
The law of causality creates a problem for the idea of miracles because it rejects the possibility that things and events can occur in ways that break the general laws of the universe and nature.
The Ashʿarites therefore denied this law in order to leave room for miracles.
It is well known that denying causal relationships between the phenomena of the material world has been one of the positions adopted by idealist philosophers in many different periods.
